items.title: 5 Things I Think I’ve Learned About The Miami Dolphins Through 10 Weeks
items.text:
It’s an evaluation season, so let’s check in and see how things are going...

Instead of reviewing the All-22 from Miami’s 24-22 loss to the Indianapolis Colts, I thought it prudent to step back and look at the big picture.
The TDLR on the film: Two bad teams played each other. One of them is “tanking” with purpose, and the other is a deeply flawed organization with little hope for the future. The Dolphins are the former.
Miami’s defense gave a spirited effort, Kyle McCord was just OK, and Zane Gonzales will become a legendary folk hero if Miami turns its franchise around with a draft slot this loss helps them secure.
While I could regale you with Chop Robinson’s impressive day or break down why McCord took bad sacks in critical spots, we’re 10 weeks into an “evaluation and rebuilding” season, so we’ve surely learned things that will shape the franchise's future.
Let’s talk about all of that because, frankly, I think it’s a lot more interesting than anything that happened against the Colts.
This might fall into “captain obvious” territory, but many head coaches are hired for their prowess on one side of the ball and struggle to maintain it when they take the head job.
It wasn’t a great start for Miami’s defense, but that unit has largely put together a respectable product for quite a while now.
The Dolphins defense ranks 10th in the NFL in yards allowed per game. That comes with the team starting a slew of rookies and second-year players at every level of the defense, and with the team’s cash spending on defense ranking last in the NFL by a comfortable margin.
Plus, the Dolphins have played the most difficult strength of schedule (by opponent winning percentage) in the NFL. They’ve faced Patrick Mahomes, Brock Purdy, Joe Burrow, Drake Maye, and Jared Goff this season.
Obviously, some of those outings went better than others, but coming out of that stretch and still sniffing the league’s top end in total defense, with the resources at their disposal, is a huge credit to Hafley and his staff.
The last feather I want to place in Hafley’s cap is that Miami’s defense hasn’t really done anything overly complex. The team isn’t static on the back end, but they’re hardly running exotic concepts.
The team has found some success with double-mug looks in recent weeks, but they haven’t even dipped their toes into the exotic Cover-2 looks Halfey used in Green Bay.
With all of those limitations, it’s genuinely impressive that Miami’s defense has managed to be a mostly middle-of-the-road unit this season.
Now, that doesn’t mean everything is perfect. “Total yards allowed” is a deeply flawed stat for several reasons. If you dig into the advanced numbers, Miami’s defense is comfortably below average.
It ranks 23rd in EPA per play and 26th in success rate allowed. The real killer has been the team’s pass defense. Miami is 28th in EPA per pass and 10th in EPA per rush—a pretty stark contrast.
I think a lot of that is due to a lack of coverage variation, athleticism, and experience. That should get better with time and offseason additions, so I’m not sounding the alarm bells despite how bad it has looked at times.
Overall, Hafley has done an excellent job with this group, which is a huge relief.

items.title: Shed catches fire in southwest Miami-Dade; downed power line complicates firefighting efforts
items.text: MIAMI-DADE COUNTY, Fla. — Firefighters responded to a shed fire in southwest Miami-Dade early Tuesday morning, where a downed power line complicated efforts to extinguish the flames, authorities said. According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, six units responded to reports of a house fire in the 16100 block of Southwest 101st Avenue at approximately 1:55 a.m. “I was awakened to like loud popping noises,” a man who lives at the home said. “When I looked out the window, I saw fire, so by then I had to yell at my family inside – my daughter – wake them up, you know, saying there’s fire. They went and grabbed the animals and brought them out front.” When firefighters arrived, they encountered heavy smoke and flames coming from a shed in the backyard of the home. Crews also discovered a downed power line near the burning structure, creating an additional safety hazard. Firefighters worked to contain the flames and prevent the fire from spreading to the main house while maintaining a safe distance from the power line, authorities said. Florida Power & Light was also called to the scene to shut off the electricity, allowing firefighters to safely extinguish the fire. “They’re scared, you know,” the resident told Local 10 News. “It’s an ongoing battle which, you know, they don’t want to be home by themselves, they can’t come outside and play because they’re scared of the power lines.” No injuries were reported. Authorities did not provide information about what caused the fire or the extent of the damage.

items.title: Miami Dolphins’ Most Valuable Player | Week Ten | Youth
items.text:
Chris Johnson has 59-yard interception return for touchdown against Colts.

The Miami Dolphins have been going through a bit of a youth-movement this season, in case you haven’t heard. They’re the youngest team in the National Football League by a wide margin — with an average age of just over 25 years at the start of the season. They’ve also had the most snaps taken by rookie players out of any NFL team this season — leading the Cleveland Browns by a comfortable amount. That emphasis on developing young players is paying off for the Dolphins in a major way. While the team is currently struggling in the standings — winning just one game on the year so far — their rookies are taking their lumps and learning the ropes at an expedited pace. That should help the team progress much quicker than most anticipate, while keeping their future cap situation in the good (and cheap) place. Miami Dolphins Week Nine MVP - Cornerback Chris Johnson One young player who has been excelling in Jeff Halfey’s defensive scheme is rookie first-rounder Chris Johnson. Miami’s young cornerback has two interceptions on the season after nabbing one against Daniel Jones of the Colts on Sunday. He returned that interception 59-yards for a touchdown — Miami’s first pick-6 on the year. In addition to his two interceptions, Johnson also has a forced fumble during his rookie campaign. Following the game, Johnson spoke about how coaching helped him make his stellar play on Sunday. > “Definitely felt good. Really just reading my keys. Once the quarterback scrambles, he’s looking to get the ball out of his hands. That’s kind of something we talked about throughout the week. When we get him off-schedule, it’s an opportunity. Really just making the most of my opportunity in that situation.” MVP TRACKER Week One - WR Caleb Douglas Week Two - LB Jacob Rodriguez Week Three - OC Aaron Brewer Week Four - EDGE Chop Robinson Week Five - RB Ollie Gordon II Week Six - BYE Week Seven - QB Malik Willis Week Eight - EDGE Chop Robinson Week Nine - EDGE Josh Uche Week Ten - CB Chris Johnson

items.title: Downed FPL power line ignited shed fire behind SW Miami-Dade property, homeowner says; no injuries reported
items.text:
SOUTHWEST MIAMI-DADE, FLA. (WSVN) - A shed behind a home in Southwest Miami-Dade caught fire overnight after a power line came down on it, the homeowner said.
7News cameras captured the flames, which erupted in the backyard of the property located near Southwest 101st Avenue and 160th Street, around 1 a.m. on Tuesday.
“I was awakened to loud popping noises,” said homeowner Rodney Kissoonlal. “So, by then, I had to yell at my family inside, my daughter, wake them up, you know, saying there’s a fire. They went and grabbed the animals and brought them out front.”
His family and pets made it out safely and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews were able to stop the flames from reaching the home.
However, Kissoonlal said he had family heirlooms and fishing gear in the shed, as well as a boat motor and BMW motorcycle that sustained extensive damage.
7News cameras captured the rubble and remains of the shed at around 7 a.m.
Kissoonlal said the fire started because a spliced Florida Power & Light power line snapped and fell onto the shed.
He said this has happened to him multiple times, the first being in 2016, which he said cost him around $300,000 in damages.
He estimated this most recent fire will cost even more in damages.
“It’s extremely frustrating. Each time there is no answers. FPL doesn’t have any answers,” said Kissoonlal.
He said his children are terrified to be in the backyard because of the fires.
“You know, they don’t want to be home by themselves. They can’t come outside and play because they’re scared of the power lines,” said Kissoonlal.
The damage from the 2016 fire cost him $300,000 without help from FPL, according to Kissoonlal.
He thinks the most recent fire will cost even more, and he hopes FPL will help him this time.
“Some sort of compensation or something. I need some answers. Fix the power line, you know, take out all these splices out of my backyard, make it somewhere safe, where my kids can come out here and enjoy themselves,” said Kissoonlal.
At around 9:00 a.m., 7News cameras captured workers cutting parts of trees to move them away from the power lines.
7News has reached out to FPL to learn what they have to say and what their protocol is.
Please check back on WSVN.com and 7News for more details on this developing story.

items.title: Flood watch in effect in Broward, Miami-Dade; isolated spots could see 10 in of rain
items.text:
NBC6’s Adam Berg has your forecast for today, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026.
A flood watch is in effect for parts of South Florida on Tuesday due to a very moist and unstable pattern that could last through at least Thursday.
The flood watch is in effect in Miami-Dade, Broward and parts of Palm Beach counties until Thursday evening as the forecast calls for multiple inches of rain. Some isolated spots could see amounts closer to 10 inches.
The combination of a front stalled just to the north and deep moisture sliding in from the west and south will keep rain chances high.
Models are a little conflicted, but the trend is for drier skies later this week and into the weekend, but this certainly bears watching.
In addition to the periods of heavy rain, we are expecting gusty winds to continue as well. We are under a small craft advisory, a high surf advisory for Broward and we also expect issues with rip currents this week.

items.title: Miami-Dade track club helping young athletes chase dreams on and off the track
items.text:
At the Goulds Panthers Track Club, the finish line is about more than winning races.

A South Miami-Dade track club is helping young athletes chase their dreams, both on and off the track. Now, the Goulds Panthers Track Club is hoping to take its talent international, giving its runners the chance to compete in Trinidad.
With Give Miami Day approaching, the community has an opportunity to help make that trip a reality. For 11 years, coach David Jacque has been helping young athletes in Goulds find their stride, but at the Goulds Panthers Track Club, the finish line is about more than winning races.
"We saw an opportunity not just to develop kids for sports, but to make an impact in their lives," said Goulds Panthers Track coach David Jacque.
Coach Jacque came to the U.S. from Trinidad on a track scholarship. Now, he's hoping to give his athletes a similar opportunity, raising money through Give Miami Day to send them to Trinidad for an international track meet.
"So that we can just better ourselves and see what's really out there in the world, and see how fast these people really are outside of Florida and outside the U.S.," said 18-year-old Rory Earle.
For Rory Earle, a high school senior hoping to earn a college scholarship, the experience could be life-changing.
"So we're very proud of our youth, we're very proud of their accomplishments, so we want to champion them, and we want to raise awareness about the important work that's happening here, so hopefully we encourage everyone to show up for them at Give Miami Day," said Julissa Rivera with the Miami Foundation.
And for these young runners, every step on the track is a step toward a future filled with possibility.
If you'd like to help these young athletes make that trip to Trinidad, Give Miami Day is Nov. 19.
You can donate as little as $25, and your gift will be matched, helping these runners get one step closer to their dreams.
You also can support the Goulds Panthers Track Club year-round through its website .

items.title: Will sports subsidies survive the Amendment 3 tax cut? Miami-Dade faces a test
items.text:
County commissioners are scheduled to vote on a multi-year funding package for the Orange Bowl football game, weeks after the tax cut passed

As local governments brace for a sharp drop in revenue after voters approved a statewide tax cut, Miami-Dade commissioners need to decide whether fiscal belt tightening will still leave room for subsidizing sporting events.
Legislation on the County Commission’s Tuesday agenda calls for extending millions of dollars of tax spending on the annual Orange Bowl college football game at Hard Rock Stadium.
This year’s budget has a $475,000 cash subsidy for the nationally televised winter matchup, and Miami-Dade also is expected to cover overtime costs for the paramedics and police officers that game organizers would otherwise need to hire for the event.
Under the legislation sponsored by Commissioner Oliver Gilbert, Miami-Dade would tentatively agree to fund the Orange Bowl through 2030 at up to $550,000 a year. That’s the same time frame when the tax cuts approved under Amendment 3 will be fully in effect — a change forecasted to strip about $700 million from the county budget.
The subsidy proposal might not have attracted much attention in prior years — the Orange Bowl is a staple of the winter tourism season, and playing host to the playoff game keeps Miami-Dade in the rotation for the coveted national championship college football game, too. Gilbert’s legislation calls the Orange Bowl and college championship “major Countywide events of significant economic impact that create tourism and provide extraordinary economic opportunities to Miami-Dade County.”
But the timing of Gilbert’s resolution sets up a commission vote on tax-funded sports expenses at the commission’s first meeting in the Amendment 3 era — after he and other county leaders warned that core services like police, fire, transit and parks will see their normal revenue sources slashed once the Amendment 3 cuts begin to take effect next fall.
Supporters of Amendment 3 on the County Commission said the measure — which shields $250,000 of a primary residence’s assessed value from non-school taxation — would bring welcome tax relief that Miami-Dade could manage by limiting spending to core services.
“By reviewing spending carefully and working together, we can prepare responsible budgets that respect taxpayers’ dollars and keep essential services strong,” Commissioner Natalie Milian Orbis said in a statement a day after the measure passed, including with a 66% yes vote from Miami-Dade voters.
Gilbert, who won a congressional seat in November and is leaving the commission in January, had no immediate response to a question about whether Miami-Dade can still afford to subsidize the Orange Bowl after the passage of Amendment 3. Gilbert campaigned against the tax-cut amendment, saying it would lead to unpopular service cuts.
Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava fought it too, and in a gloomy note to county employees after Election Day, she signalled an austerity era was coming to Miami-Dade government.
“We cannot minimize what the passage of Amendment 3 means for our ability to deliver the services our residents depend on,” she wrote in the Nov. 4 email . “The road ahead will require difficult choices.”
